economics-of-rejection-and-termination-t.text: Economics of rejection and termination: the design the model states.

This page records the operator's economic design for the registry as the Lean model will state it, the amounts that move in every outcome, the attacks the mechanism prices and the ones it cannot. It is the design behind the theorem list and the paper; it changes no code. Rulings are quoted as the operator gave them in the decisions and the mandate.

story.text: As a scientist reviewing the registry's economics, I read one page and learn which amounts a requester, a processor and the treasury pay or receive in each outcome, which parameters a creator sets, and which attacks the design prices or leaves unpriced, so that I can judge every claim the paper makes before it is written and see which are proved and which are not.

the-rulings.text: Operator, 13 October 2026, in his words: "provable rejection must be punished but not with the deposit"; "it's a new parameter bond"; "termination should pay the treasury"; on the order of work: "what I want is the lean model done, and from it the full economic system explained in a paper, so I get a review now"; and "the paper will be reviewed by a scientist; do not gloss over details". The adopted design, as the desk worded it for planning:
A registry parameter, the bond, carried by every request beside its deposit.
A rejection forfeits the bond only on a fault proved against the root the request recorded at booking. Without that proof, a rejection refunds deposit and bond.
The tip pays the processor for the slot on every rejection, as on a fold.
The forfeited bond is split between the proving processor and the treasury (a treasury donation); the split is a registry parameter set at creation, beside the bond.
Rejection on expiry returns the bond.
A registry parameter, the termination fee: a fold that terminates a key donates at least the fee to the treasury; the terminate request carries it.

Also adopted: the registry parameters are set at creation and never changed by a fold; a fold, a retraction and an exit by expiry return the bond to the owner; the owner's refund of the deposit and the approval holds on every rejection; the treasury donation is a transaction field that the model owes.

one-request-every-outcome.text: The diagram is the whole set of outcomes: five, the same five the paper tabulates. A fault is a lifecycle mismatch at booking: the request's edge has no successor from the leaf its key held in the state with root R, which includes a request that names an excluded edge.

where-each-amount-goes.text: Amounts: deposit, bond, tip, termination fee. The processor's share of a forfeited bond is the floor of the split times the bond; the treasury receives the rest, so the two always add up to the bond exactly. What the model owes is a floor to the owner and a floor to the treasury; the processor keeps what the request held beyond those floors, so its gain is bounded by conservation, never stated as a payment.

Three facts the table fixes. The tip is returned on a retraction and paid to the processor on everything else, so an honest requester whose request is rejected without proof or on expiry loses the tip. A zero donation cannot be written on the ledger (the donation field is a positive amount), so a zero treasury share or a zero termination fee means the field is left out; the model's donation obligation applies only when the owed amount is positive. And the fee of a termination is owed per terminated key, so a batch of terminations owes the fee times their number.

the-fault-proof.text: The request records the root of the state it read at booking. A rejection that claims the forfeit carries the whole logical map whose commitment is that root, and the model checks that the commitment of the supplied map equals the recorded root and that the request's edge has no successor from the leaf the supplied map holds at the key. This is the authenticated logical read the rejection evidence already uses, one state earlier. Collision resistance of the commitment is a named assumption of the model, and every honesty theorem is stated under it. The processor chooses the ground: a rejection on the expiry ground never forfeits; a rejection on the mismatch ground forfeits exactly when its fault proof holds. A mismatch that arose after booking (another key holder folded first) has no fault proof, so the requester keeps the bond.

what-the-creator-sets-and-what-the-model.text: What the creator sets, and what the model will constrain.

The paper derives each constraint as an inequality with a worked example in lovelace. The ones the design already implies: the treasury share of one forfeited bond must exceed the cost a flood is meant to carry; the processor share plus the tip must cover the processor's cost of a rejection, or faults wait for expiry; the tip alone must cover a processor's share of a fold; the split must stay below one or a requester who rejects its own faulty request pays nothing; the fee must exceed the value of holding a key terminal. Each constraint names the model definition it is read from.

what-the-design-prices-and-what-it-does-.text: What the design prices, and what it does not.

honest-limits-stated-up-front.text: The model has floors and conservation, not fees, execution units or markets. Costs in lovelace are real; the value of a key, opportunity cost and fee volatility are outside the model, so claims that involve them are derived by hand from proved transfer lemmas and labelled so. An honest requester loses no deposit and no bond, but may lose the tip, and after the reclaim window has closed has no way to leave the queue on its own: it depends on a processor's incentive to reject. The correspondence between this model and the validators is evidenced by the conformance suite, not proved, and is named as an assumption.
